source.title: Dimension independent excess risk by stochastic gradient descent
source.authors: X. Chen; Qiang Liu; Xin T. Tong

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. Its title differs slightly from the supplied metadata title; no other file problem is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The authors explicitly argue that their SGD settings do not exhibit the double-descent phenomenon, attributing this to implicit regularization and ridge regularization. Their own dimension-sweep simulations report generalization-error trends, but do not trace a curve through an interpolation threshold.
record.gate_note: The paper does not directly sweep model size through an interpolation threshold, training epochs, or sample size to measure double descent. Its theoretical bounds and the cited double-descent results from other papers are not rows. The six rows below capture its own dimension-sweep simulations; they show dimension-dependent generalization behavior but do not measure the fall-rise-fall behavior named by any claim version. V4 is marked tested_not_extracted because of the authors' specific argument against double descent, but no row directly measures that curve, so no version labels are assigned.
record.test_reason: This is a theory paper on dimension-free generalization bounds for single-pass SGD with ridge regularization. It mentions double descent only in related work (Section 1.2), asserting that implicit and ridge regularization mean 'we do not have the double descent phenomenon'. This is an assertion, not a measured test. None of its simulations traces test error through an interpolation threshold for an interpolating learner. Single-pass SGD over N=500 samples never fits the training set, and λ is fixed at 0.01 rather than optimally tuned. So no version's effect, including V6's claim that the peak disappears under optimal regularization, is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right, but the double-descent remark sits in related work (Section 1.2), not in the conclusion. The conclusion states that overparameterization need not cause overfitting when effective dimension is low. It adds that ambient dimension is a poor indicator of model complexity.
record.recipe_differences: The paper develops theoretical generalization bounds for SGD and reports dimension-sweep simulations in linear regression; it does not reproduce the original double-descent curve protocol.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported dimension trends differ with the predictor covariance spectrum: decaying spectra are described as stable, while constant spectra show overfitting. The authors also attribute their absence of double descent to implicit regularization and ridge regularization, but do not isolate or sweep those choices.

fits_no_version.finding: For single-pass ridge SGD in linear regression, generalization error is described as flat in ambient dimension p, including p ≫ N, when the covariance spectrum decays. It rises with p when the spectrum is flat.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under low effective dimension (trace-bounded covariance), SGD generalization error is independent of ambient dimension, even when p ≫ N.

fits_no_version.finding: Adding redundant features leaves error stable if their total variance is bounded, and causes overfitting if Σz = I.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether redundant features hurt SGD generalization depends on tr(Σz), not on their count.

record.problems: The simulations report qualitative trends rather than numerical results in the text, and their plotted sweeps do not measure a curve around an interpolation threshold. The paper reports no direct deep-network size sweep, epoch-wise sweep, or sample-size sweep for double descent.

untested.parts: No deep-network size sweep. The two-layer NN section is theory only.
No sweep of an interpolating learner past the interpolation point.
No peak-location prediction. 'Low effective dimension' is used for bounds, not to locate peaks.
No measured peak, no noise variation, no tuned-regularization comparison. The absence of double descent is only asserted, citing Nakkiran et al. 2020.
No curve plotted against an effective parameter count.

record.verdict_notes: The record's T5 is too strong. The authors do not argue any version is wrong; they attribute the absence of a peak to regularization, which is consistent with V6, and cite others for it. Figures 1(a), 1(c) and 2(a) cross p = N = 500 with no rise described. This is only weakly suggestive, because the learner never interpolates and λ is not tuned, so it is not treated as a V6 test.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network model-size sweep and test error around the size that just fits the training set.
Test error over training epochs or other training-time sweep.
Sample-size sweep near an interpolation threshold.

No direct capacity sweep through an interpolation point or measurement of a second descent. The authors argue against double descent in their SGD and regularization setting, but the reported simulations do not establish the curve's shape.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
No test of noise-driven or multiple peaks, or of whether optimally tuned regularization removes a measured peak.
No comparison of the curve against an effective parameter count.

rows.subject: linear regression model (28)

rows.measure: Generalization error G(w), mean and standard deviation over repetitions
rows.uncertainty: Standard deviation is described as plotted; numerical value not stated.
rows.note: The text says generalization error does not increase as dimension increases. That trend is not a measurement of a fall-rise-fall curve.
rows.check: Figure-only. p sweeps 100–1000 across N=500, but the learner is single-pass SGD with λ=0.01 and never interpolates. The lack of an increase is not a test of a peak at an interpolation threshold.
